# A model for developing AI pedagogical and content knowledge in inservice and preservice non-STEM 

### elementary teachers

**Ya-Ching Fan1** [** ·**](http://orcid.org/0000-0001-9457-6489) **Bor-Chen Kuo2** [** ·**](http://orcid.org/0000-0003-1741-2450) **Pei-Chen Wu2** [** ·**](http://orcid.org/0009-0000-1343-5407) **Chen-Huei Liao3**

Received: 3 June 2025 / Accepted: 29 September 2025 © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2025

**Abstract** Rapid advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have transformed instruction and learning. This study developed and evaluated a nationwide teacher training model for enhancing the AI knowledge, AI pedagogical knowledge, AI content knowledge, and AI pedagogical and content knowledge (AIPACK) of inservice and preservice elementary teachers (ISETs and PSETs, respectively) with non-STEM backgrounds. The study applied a quasi-experimental design and included 31 ISETs and 28 PSETs who participated in an 18-hr training program covering basic knowledge about AI, AI-driven technologies, AI tools, AI platforms, and strategies for integrating AI into subject-specific teaching. The participants’ AIPACK was assessed before and after training by using pretests and posttests of AIPACK questionnaire. The findings validated the effectiveness of the AIPACK model. The results revealed no signifi- cant difference in the pretest and posttest AIPACK scores between the ISETs and PSETs but significant improvements in all dimensions of AIPACK in both groups after training. This study also discussed the implications of the AIPACK training model for professional development, teacher education, and potential directions for future research in the era of AI.

**Keywords** Artificial intelligence · Elementary teacher · Inservice teacher · Preservice teacher · Technological pedagogical content knowledge

**1 Introduction**

Rapid advances in generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) have revolutionized education. Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven technologies and tools have been effec- tively applied in educational settings across the globe, with applications in K–12 

Extended author information available on the last page of the article education being particularly successful (Mishra et al., 2023; United Nations Educa- tional, Scientific and Cultural Organization \[UNESCO\], 2024). GenAI can transform instructional practices, classroom interactions, and assessment methods (Searson et al., 2024). Recognizing the potential of AI to promote greater equity, personalization, and quality in education (UNESCO, 2021), UNESCO released its _Guidance for Gen-_ _erative AI in Education and Research_ in 2023 to address the use of GenAI in lesson planning, instructional design, and resource creation. UNESCO (2024) subsequently proposed an _AI Competency Framework for Teachers_, which clearly defines the com- petencies that teachers must possess in the era of AI. This framework suggests that training programs to assist teachers in progressing from acquiring content to creating content must integrate five dimensions of AI competency: a human-centered mind- set, AI ethics, AI foundations and applications, AI pedagogy, and AI for professional development (PD).

In Taiwan, the Ministry of Education (MOE) has similarly encouraged the integra- tion of AI into instruction. The MOE developed its _Digital Teaching Guidelines 3.0_ to elucidate how to incorporate cutting-edge AI technologies and best practices into classroom instruction. These guidelines support teachers in integrating age-appropri- ate AI technologies and tools into instructional design and assessment (MOE, 2024). The MOE also developed and implemented the Taiwan Adaptive Learning Platform (TALPer), a GenAI learning companion, to enhance teaching and learning directly (Fig. 1).

Although AI-driven tools are promising teaching and learning aids, their appli- cation in classrooms poses several challenges for teachers (Ning et al., 2024). For example, studies have demonstrated that many teachers do not possess the skills required to use AI-driven tools (Kim et al., 2021) some teachers also experience anxi-

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 1** MOE AI learning companion ety when learning concepts associated with AI, such as machine learning and data- driven decision-making (Celik, [2023)](#references). AI is a novel technology for both students and teachers in K–12 settings, and most teachers in Taiwan do not receive formal training in AI during their teacher preparation programs. This lack of preparation is concern- ing because one study indicated that teachers cannot successfully implement AI in instruction without adequate preparation (Kim & Kwon, [2023)](#references).

Teachers who possess AI pedagogical and content knowledge (AIPACK) can make more informed decisions regarding instructional design than those who lack such knowledge can. Koehler and Mishra (2009) proposed a technological pedagogi- cal and content knowledge (TPACK) framework for training teachers to integrate technology into instruction; this framework was developed on the basis of Shulman’s (1986) pedagogical content knowledge (PCK) theory. The TPACK framework posits that the effective integration of technology into pedagogy requires teachers to possess an integrated knowledge of technology, pedagogy, and content (Wang et al., [2018)](#authors-and-affiliations). Extending the TPACK framework, Celik ([2023)](#references) theorized that intelligent TPACK requires AI knowledge (AIK), AI content knowledge (AICK), AI pedagogical knowl- edge (AIPK), and AIPACK, arguing that such knowledge is crucial to teaching in the era of AI.

Training programs on applying AI in education are essential for elementary school teachers. The present study adopted the _AI Competency Framework for Teachers_ (UNESCO, 2024) and intelligent TPACK (Celik, [2023)](#references) as theoretical frameworks to develop an AIPACK teacher training model. This model integrates AIK, AICK, AIPK, and AIPACK to cultivate AI competencies among in-service elementary school teachers (ISETs) and preservice elementary school teachers (PSETs). The AIPACK training model was designed to foster high-quality AI competencies, pro- vide opportunities for practicing AI-integrated instruction, and enhance teachers’ readiness to apply AI in the classroom. Having established the AIPACK model, this study addressed the following research questions:

1. What are the ISETs and PSETs’ initial knowledge of AIK, AICK, AIPK, and AIPACK before training?
2. What is the effectiveness of the AIPACK training model for improving the AIK, AICK, AIPK, and AIPACK of ISETs and PSETs?
3. What are the differences in the improvements of AIK, AICK, AIPK, and AIPACK between ISETs and PSETs?

Research has yet to examine practical training in AIPACK for teachers outside the disciplines of Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM). To address this gap, the present study developed a teacher training model designed to provide PSETs and ISETs with AI-specific technological knowledge (TK), pedagogical knowledge (PK), subject-specific content knowledge (CK), and PCK. Through this model, this study addressed the urgent need for struc- tured AI training in teacher education to assist teachers in integrating AI into subject-specific instruction.

**2 Literature review**

**2.1 Theoretical framework: TPACK and AIPACK**

Professional knowledge for teachers has been conceptualized using several inter- related frameworks. For example, Shulman (1986) proposed three domains of pro- fessional knowledge with which a teacher must be thoroughly familiar: general PK, subject-specific CK, and PCK. Koehler and Mishra (2009) broadened these domains into the TPACK framework by integrating TK into the model (Chai et al., [2013;](#references) Rosenberg & Koehler, 2015; Yao, [2021)](#authors-and-affiliations). The TPACK framework posits that effec- tive teaching through technology requires teachers to combine TK, PK, and CK to design explanations, demonstrations, and activities that enhance student engagement and understanding. Studies have consistently demonstrated that PSET TPACK can be strengthened through opportunities for practice and guided teaching experiences (Kaya & Dag, [2013;](#references) Zhan et al., [2013)](#authors-and-affiliations), and that TK is pivotal to developing TPACK (Kabakci Yurdakul & Coklar, [2014;](#references) Mouza et al., 2014). As AI becomes increasingly prevalent, researchers are extending TPACK to AI-specific domains. A growing body 

| of research on  | teacher education has indicated that AIPACK  | can be employed  | to  |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: |
| cultivate AI-specific competencies in instructors (Celik,  | [2023;](#references) |  Kim & Kwon,  | [2023;](#references) |
| Velander et al., | [2024)](#authors-and-affiliations). The UNESCO _AI Competency Framework for Teachers_ |  ( | 2024) |

suggests that effective AI integration requires teachers to prioritize human flourishing, adhere to ethical standards and regulations, apply conceptual and practical AI skills, employ AI to support pedagogy and student interactions, and use AI for continual professional growth. These skills require teachers to possess technical knowledge and the ability to apply AI ethically, responsibly, and pedagogically. Several researchers have proposed extensions to and interpretations of the AIPACK framework applica- ble to teacher education. For example, Celik ([2023)](#references) developed an intelligent TPACK scale comprising intelligent TK, intelligent technological pedagogical knowledge (TPK), intelligent technological CK (TCK), intelligent TPACK, and ethics. Their findings revealed that intelligent TK helped teachers make more informed decisions regarding the implementation of AI, although instructor self-confidence regarding CK, AIK, and AIPK was low. Despite these challenges, studies have indicated that AI-specific TPK is crucial to the effective integration of AI into instructional practice (Celik, [2023;](#references) Seufert et al., 2021). Similarly, Lorenz and Romeike (2023) developed an AIPACK framework on the basis of a digital pedagogical and content knowledge model; this framework comprises AIPK, AICK, and AIPCK as core competencies in teacher PD training. Moreover, Kim and Kwon ([2023)](#references) examined South Korean elementary school teachers’ experiences in using AI in their curricula; they reported that teachers had the least confidence in AICK, followed by TK and AIPK. Notably, a solid foundation in AICK was associated with reduced instructional anxiety. These findings suggest that AI competencies must be contextualized in terms of CK and PK. Furthermore, Velander et al. ([2024)](#authors-and-affiliations) proposed that teachers typically have limited AITK, which often results in misconceptions regarding AI and visceral reactions to AI shaped by these misconceptions. Additionally, although the participants in the aforementioned studies were aware of the ethical implications of AI, they struggled to articulate the technical reasons underlying their concerns. Furthermore, teach-

ers often experience fear, anxiety, and low confidence when asked to integrate AI into instruction that result from misconceptions, limited knowledge, and a perceived lack of control over the development of AI (Kim & Kwon, [2023;](#references) Velander et al., [2024)](#authors-and-affiliations). TPACK provides a foundational framework for understanding how teachers can integrate technology into teaching by combining TK, PK, and CK. Developed by Koehler and Mishra (2009), TPACK primarily addresses the integration of gen- eral digital technologies and has been extensively applied to support technology use in K–12 education. The AIPACK framework extends TPACK to the applications of AI in education by integrating AICK, AIPK, and AIPCK with ethical and affective dimensions. AIPACK integrates the competencies teachers require to implement AI in instruction responsibly and effectively (Celik, [2023;](#references) UNESCO, 2024). To address teachers’ lack of competencies in implementing AI-integrated instruction, the pres- ent study adopted the AI Competency Framework for Teachers (UNESCO, 2024) and intelligent TPACK (Celik, [2023)](#references) as its theoretical foundations. The proposed AIPACK framework conceptualizes teachers’ AI professional competencies as con- sisting of AIK (including ethics), AIPK, AICK, and AIPACK.

**2.2 Implementation of TPACK and AIPACK in teacher education**

In teacher education, the TPACK framework has been extensively adopted to design PD programs that support teachers in integrating technology into instruction (Angeli et al., [2016;](#references) Kim et al., 2021; Oda et al., 2020; Zhang & Tang, [2021)](#authors-and-affiliations). TPACK-based PD programs enhance ISET knowledge and classroom practices (Hong & Stonier, [2015;](#references) Oda et al., 2020). For example, Angeli et al. ([2016)](#references) prepared K–6 teachers to teach computational thinking through a TPACK-based PD program, and Oda et al. (2020) demonstrated that geographic information system integration in science and social studies curricula considerably increased after teachers participated in TPACK- based PD.

Proper modeling in teacher education programs can enhance the development of TPACK in PSETs (Tokmak et al., 2013; Young et al., [2013)](#authors-and-affiliations). First-year PSETs fre- quently lack a foundation in TK, PK, and TPK (Valtonen et al., 2011). Additionally, UNESCO (2024) indicated that gaining proficiency in one domain can positively influence proficiency in another domain; this finding suggests that acquiring a com- prehensive understanding of AI may enhance teachers’ ability to implement AI-driven instruction. Nevertheless, because GenAI is an emerging technology, most K–12 teachers have not received formal training in its use (Xia et al., [2022)](#authors-and-affiliations). Moreover, research conducted in several countries has revealed that elementary school teachers are unprepared to integrate AI into their instruction. For example, studies conducted in South Korea (Kim & Kwon, [2023)](#references), and China (Sun et al., 2023) have indicated the need for enhanced teacher training and PD programs to support AI integration into education. However, PD programs that instruct teachers in the use of AI in instruction are lacking, limiting opportunities to acquire the competencies and skills required to integrate AI into K–12 classroom education (Velander et al., [2024)](#authors-and-affiliations). Therefore, designing a PD model to teach AI skills is an essential task for teacher educators. Kim et al. (2021) employed the TPACK framework to identify the competencies required for computer science teachers to effectively implement AI instruction in 

K–12 settings. Subsequently, Kim and Kwon ([2023)](#references) developed an AI competency survey on the basis of the TPACK framework and examined the experiences of South Korean elementary school teachers in using AI in instruction. However, these studies neither designed a PD program grounded in the TPACK framework nor evaluated the effectiveness of the framework in promoting the development of teachers’ AI-specific competencies. Nevertheless, some studies have proposed models that have effectively applied the TPACK framework to AI and developed teachers’ AI-specific skills and knowledge. For example, a TPACK-based PD program, TPACKAI, was developed by Sun et al. (2023) for K–12 computer science teachers. TPACKAI combines AI con- tent, pedagogy, and technology through programming tasks, robotics, instructional design, and hands-on practice. The TPACKAI program encompasses AI-specific CK, TCK, PCK, TPK, and TPACK. To evaluate the effectiveness of TPACKAI, Sun et al. (2023) conducted a quasi-experimental study with 40 computer science ISETs. The 25-day, 75-hr program comprised face-to-face sessions (10 days, 45 h) and online activities (15 days, 30 h). The results indicated that participation in the TPACKAI pro- gram substantially increased teachers’ AIK, teaching skills, and self-efficacy. Kong et al. (2024) developed a 6-hr TPACK-based PD course for 191 primary school ISETs to increase their competency in integrating AI and Internet of Things (IoT) applica- tions into STEM activities. The course introduced core AI concepts and the IoT and cultivated teachers’ problem-solving and digital creativity. The results revealed that 81.15% of the participants demonstrated an acceptable level of digital creativity, as reflected in their IoT system designs, many of which integrated AI elements. The aforementioned models demonstrate the value of integrating hands-on experience into the assessment and development of AI-specific competencies.

Although AIPACK is increasingly recognized as a critical framework in teacher education (Celik, [2023;](#references) Kim & Kwon, [2023;](#references) Lorenz & Romeike, 2023; Velander et al., [2024)](#authors-and-affiliations), few PD programs have implemented and examined AIPACK outside of STEM education. By contrast, TPACK-based PD is well-established in non-STEM disciplines. The present study addressed this gap by proposing an AIPACK-based PD model that supports ISETs and PSETs in non-STEM fields at the elementary level. This PD assists teachers in implementing subject-specific instruction, reviews salient ethical considerations, and provides authentic opportunities for integrating AI in instruction.

**2.3 AIPACK teacher training model**

Teacher PD is a transformative process that involves authentic experiences, reflec- tion, and social interactions (Zaslavsky & Leikin, [2004)](#authors-and-affiliations). Although programs such as TPACKAI (Sun et al., 2023) and the PD program developed by Kong et al. (2024) have successfully cultivated AI-specific teaching skills, they have primarily targeted computer science or STEM teachers. To date, the literature has yet to detail training opportunities in AI instruction for general elementary school teachers. Nevertheless, these teachers must possess the ability to design age-appropriate activities, provide learning support, and appropriately integrate AI and other technological tools into their pedagogy. In Taiwan, elementary schools follow a homeroom-based teaching system in which teachers are responsible for teaching multiple subjects. This struc-

ture requires teacher educators to empower elementary school teachers with AIPACK competencies across disciplines.

To address this need, the present study designed an AIPACK-based PD program to cultivate the AI competencies of ISETs and PSETs and enhance instruction in Chinese, mathematics, and the natural sciences. The PD program was evaluated in terms of the AIK, AIPK, AICK, and AIPACK components of the present study’s AIPACK framework (Fig. 2). AIK refers to the knowledge of the fundamental AI concepts and skills required to use AI-driven technologies and includes knowledge of the ethical implications of GenAI. AICK refers to the ability to use diverse AI- driven tools to support subject-specific instruction, such as the ability to use AI tools to identify plant and animal species in a natural science classroom. AIPK refers to the application of AI-driven tools in general, non-subject-specific teaching activities in alignment with instructional objectives and teaching approaches. Teachers must also understand the potential and limitations of AI-driven tools in the classroom, such as in generating formative assessments. Finally, AIPACK refers to the ability to integrate AI into subject-specific instructional design on the basis of subject CK and teaching models (e.g., using AI to facilitate inquiry-based learning in science). In this 

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 2** AIPACK framework study, the participating teachers learned from six expert teachers who demonstrated how to deliver AIPACK-based instruction across six subjects. This approach enabled the participants to replicate best practices and contextualize AI integration within their own teaching.

The proposed model incorporated hands-on, subject-specific practice and inter- disciplinary applications, enabling teachers to observe, practice, and adapt AIPACK- based lessons in subjects such as Chinese, mathematics, and the natural sciences. These hands-on activities also ensured applicability to authentic teaching contexts. By embedding AIPACK into elementary teacher education, the model extends the lit- erature and directly addresses the identified gap in PD design. Overall, the AIPACK model proposed in this study provides a theoretically grounded, practical framework for cultivating AI competencies in elementary teacher education.

**3 Methodology**

**3.1 Participants**

In total, 31 ISETs and 28 PSETs participated in this study. The ISETs were invited from elementary schools from counties and cities across Taiwan and participated in a summer PD program titled “Artificial Intelligence Pedagogical and Content Knowl- edge” at a Taiwanese teacher education university. Participation in the program was voluntary. Because the ISETs hailed from different regions of Taiwan, they could only attend an intensive PD course during summer or winter vacation, whereas the PSETs completed the course as part of their regular semester curriculum. Owing to venue size limitations, only 31 non-STEM ISETs were included; they represented 22 elementary schools across northern, central, and southern Taiwan (Table 1). The

PSETs were enrolled in a course entitled “Digital Learning” as part of an elemen- tary teacher preparation program. The aim of this course was to provide PSETs with practical experience in integrating technology into their teaching and to develop their ability to use technology to support elementary school students’ learning. Among the 31 ISETs, 12 were men (38.71%), and 19 were women (61.29%). Moreover, 5 had a bachelor’s degree (16.13%), and 26 had a master’s degree (83.87%). 4 had less than 5 years of teaching experience (12.9%), 4 had 5 to less than 10 years (12.9%), 5 had 11 to less than 15 years (16.13%), 6 had 16 to less than 20 years (19.35%), and 12 had 20 years or more (38.71%). Among the 28 PSETs, 13 were men (46.43%), and 15 were women (53.57%); all of them were undergraduates in their senior year. The PSETs majored in a non-STEM, education-related subject, and the ISETs had bach- elor’s degrees in non-STEM majors.

**3.2 Research design and procedures**

A quasi-experimental study employing a nonequivalent groups pretest-posttest design was conducted to assess the effectiveness of the AIPACK teacher training model in improving the AIPACK of the ISETs (31 in an experimental group) and PSETs (28 in a control group). The training program for the ISETs involved 18 h of class time over 2.5 days, and the course for the PSETs had 18 h of class time over 6 weeks. All participants were instructed using the same instructional methods and materi- als (Table [2)](#33-instruments-and-materials). In the first hour of class, the teacher educator explained the purpose of the training model and signed the ethics permit. An AIPACK questionnaire was then administered to the participants as a pretest to assess their initial AIPACK. The training program was conducted face-to-face, with each participant using either their own or a university-provided tablet or laptop. The AIPACK training proceeded in the following five stages. (1) The teacher educator provided an overview of concepts in TPACK and AIPACK (2) In the AIK stage, in the first hour of the program, the teacher educator focused on AIK and introduced technologies and concepts in AI, such as machine learning and natural language processing. The participants also received instruction on the application of common AI-driven tools in daily life through an online video. (3) In the AIPK stage, for 6 h of the lessons, two modeling expert K–12 ISETs introduced several general AI-driven tools, platforms, and resources that can be integrated into instruction and learning. (4) In the AICK stage, for 9 h of the lesson, three modeling expert ISETs introduced how AI can be integrated into Chi- nese, mathematics, and natural science instruction. The participants also engaged in hands-on activities. Table 3 provides an example of TALPer integration into natural science lesson plans during the hands-on activity design segment of the AICK phase of the program. Finally, (5) in the AIPACK stage, in a final 1-hr online session, six experts ISETs provided 10-min instructional videos (totaling 60 min) on how AI can be integrated into elementary school instruction on Chinese, English, mathematics, the natural science, the arts, and special education. At the end of the program, all participants completed the AIPACK questionnaire again as a posttest.

### 3.3 Instruments and materials

This study utilized a set of learning materials and a questionnaire developed by the authors. The following subsections provide the details.

1. AIPACK Questionnaire.

**Table 3** Example of integrating TALPer into natural science lesson plans during the AICK phase of hands- on activity design

Integrating Generative AI Into Natural Science Lesson Plans Unit name Effects of Heat Transfer on Matter

Grade Fifth grade (age 11) Course topics Thermos Design: Human Brain vs. AI Brain

Course objective 1. To understand the basic principles of thermoses, specifically heat conduction, convection, and radiation.

2. To explore the difference between AI and human reasoning in designing and predicting the thermal conductivity of thermoses.
3. To cultivate students’ skills in hands-on practice, teamwork, and scientific inquiry. Preparation 6 tablets, 1 roll of aluminium foil, 6 pieces of nonwoven fabric, 20 paper cups, 20 

plastic cups, 20 plastic cup lids, 6 pairs of scissors Activities (2 h Students log on to TALPer and access the tablets to ensure that all can interact with 50 min) the GenAI assistant. (10 min)

The teacher displays thermoses made of different materials and asks the students: How does a thermos maintain its temperature? What factors influence its thermal performance? Can GenAI help us solve this problem? Through group discussion, the teacher stimulates curiosity and introduces the day’s activity: investigating and constructing thermos cups and comparing human vs. GenAI designs. (10 min) Group Experiment

Students are provided with materials and work in groups of six to facilitate col- laborative learning. Each group first constructs a thermos using human reasoning and subsequently employs GenAI to produce an AI-generated thermos design. The students record the key factors in both designs and illustrate the thermos designs on a mini whiteboard. (30 min)

On the basis of the designs generated through human reasoning and those generated by AI, the students construct thermos prototypes corresponding to both the human- designed and the GenAI-designed versions. Hot water is poured into each prototype, and the temperature is measured at 0, 2, 4, 6, and 8 min. The data are collected systematically, and the results are displayed on mini whiteboards. (60 min) Each group presents their experimental results and engages in discussion. The teacher guides the students to consider the following questions: Which design fac- tors most strongly influence thermos performance? How can human and AI design principles be combined? Finally, the teacher synthesizes the discussion by reinforc- ing the scientific concepts of heat transfer (conduction, convection, and radiation) and assigns homework for further practice. (60 min)

The focus of the training program in this study was to enable ISETs and PSETs to attain AIPACK and several components of AIPACK, namely, AIK, AICK, AIPK, and AIPACK. The AIPACK questionnaire established in this study was used to assess the AIPACK of ISETs and PSETs, and it was designed on the basis of the intelligent- TPACK framework proposed by Celik ([2023)](#references) and the TPACK framework devel- oped by Koehler and Mishra (2009). The questionnaire items were developed by the authors in another study and demonstrated strong reliability. Specifically, the overall scale and the AIK, AICK, AIPK, and AIPACK subscales had reliability coefficients of 0.98, 0.88, 0.94, 0.95, and 0.95, respectively. The content validity of the question- naire items was confirmed through three rounds of expert reviews conducted by six scholars with expertise in TPACK, digital learning, educational measurement and statistics, and AI in education. The experts evaluated whether the items were worded clearly, were appropriately distributed, and adequately covered the concepts they were designed to measure. The questionnaire inquired into the teachers’ background characteristics, teaching experience, and AIPACK. In total, 26 items pertained to overall AIPACK, and 7, 6, 7, and 6 of these items pertained to AIK, AICK, AIPK, and AIPACK, respectively; these items were rated on a 5-point Likert scale with end- points ranging from 1 _(strongly disagree)_ to 5 _(strongly agree)_.

2. Design of AIPACK Content for Training.

The AIPACK content in the training program taught the teachers how to use AI- driven tools, platforms, or resources to integrate AI into subject-specific instruction to enhance teaching effectiveness. The online learning materials were developed with reference to educational literature regarding AIPACK and to the basic AI concepts proposed by Celik ([2023)](#references) and UNESCO (2024). In addition, two experts in education and information technology selected the AI concepts they considered most crucial for teachers and designed instructional materials based on these concepts. To ensure con- tent validity, the learning materials were reviewed by two faculty members who had considerable experience in the design and implementation of AI education for use with K–12 students. The online reference materials covered AIK, AICK, AIPK, and AIPACK. The AIK-related content provided an overview of the TPACK framework, clarifying the relationship between AI, technology, and TPACK. Participants also received instruction on the general principles underlying AI, the workings behind various AI-driven tools, and ethical issues in AI. The AIPK-related content provided participants with an introduction to the AI resources that can be integrated into educa- tion. These resources included the MOE AI platform and ChatGPT, Napkin, Magic- School, Suno, Gamma, Midjourney, Copilot, and Claude for generating lesson plans, text-based material, test items, songs, images, and mind maps. The AICK-related content was on the AI-driven tools that can be used for subject-specific education. The program also provided an introduction to integrating AI-driven tools into Chi- nese, mathematics, and natural sciences classes. Specifically, the teachers in training learned about how AI can be used to contextualize images and grade written essays in Chinese lessons, create equations with solutions for mathematics lessons, and out- line the steps in experimental design for inquiry-based and practical science lessons. The AIPACK-related content comprised six videos on subject-specific instructional models. For example, the videos covered how CoolE Bot (an AI chatbot for learning English) can be used for automated grading and speech recognition to enhance the student’s written and oral abilities in English. The videos also covered how the MOE AI learning companion can be integrated into the 5E scientific inquiry model to allow students to explore experimental designs, explain and elaborate on the experimental results obtained, and improve their ability to engage in scientific argumentation.

**3.4 Data collection and analysis**

The pretest and posttest AIPACK scores were collected and analyzed using descrip- tive statistical analysis, one-sample _t_-tests, independent-sample _t_-tests, dependent- sample _t_-tests, and one-way analysis of covariance, and effect sizes. With regard to descriptive statistics, the means and standard deviations of the pretest and posttest 

AIPACK scores of the participants are presented. One-sample _t_-tests were used to ana- lyze the initial AIPACK of the participants on each item. Independent-sample _t_-tests were used to analyze differences in pretest and posttest AIPACK scores between the ISETs and PSETs. Effect sizes of 0.2, 0.5, and 0.8 indicated small, medium, and large effects, respectively, and were compared between the two groups (Cohen, [1988)](#references). Dependent-sample _t_-tests were used to analyze differences between pretest versus posttest AIPACK scores for both groups. One-way analysis of covariance was used to analyze differences between the ISETs and PSETs in mean posttest scores.

**4 Results**

**4.1 Prior AIPACK**

To measure the prior AIPACK of the ISETs and PSETs, we assessed the pretest AIPACK scores for the participants before training. The descriptive statistics for the initial AIPACK scores of the participants are presented in Table 4. The one-sample _t_-tests revealed that the mean initial AIPACK scores of the participants, particularly the scores for items related to AIK, were significantly greater than 3.5 on most items; this indicates that the participants possessed sufficient prior AIK. The only AIK item for which the participants demonstrated insufficient understanding was “understand basic programming principles that are applied in the development of AI-driven tools.” In addition, the participants also had insufficient AIPK regarding the item “select appropriate AI-driven tools for classroom management” and AIPACK regard- ing the item “take a leadership role among my colleagues in facilitating lesson plan- ning activities with AI-driven tools.” The AIPACK pretest scores of the participants are presented in Table 5. The independent t-test revealed that the ISETs and PSETs did not significantly differ in their mean scores on the four dimensions of AIPACK (AIK: _t_ = 0.44, _p_ \>.05; AICK: _t_ = 0.36, _p_ \>.05; AIPK: _t_ = 0.17, _p_ \>.05; AIPCK: _t_ = 0.26, _p_ \>.05). The results indicated that the ISETs and PSETs had similar pretest levels of AIPACK.

### 5 Discussion and conclusions

This study determined the effectiveness of the AIPACK training model in an intensive PD workshop for inservice teachers and in a teacher education preparatory course for preservice teachers. The training model was implemented to enhance the ISETs’ and PSETs’ AI-related knowledge and competencies to improve their ability to integrate AI-driven technologies and tools into subject-specific teaching. During the training, all participants acquired AIPACK. The AIPACK training model led to significant improvements in AIK, AICK, AIPK, and AIPACK. Three possible reasons explain the AIPACK model’s effectiveness.

### First, the AIPACK training model provided procedural scaffolding in the partici- pants’ process of understanding how AI can be integrated into subject-specific teach- ing. The four phases of the AIPACK model also enabled the participants to acquire

AIK, AICK, AIPK, and AIPACK. Studies have indicated that TPACK development is strongly correlated with TK and that TK can predict this development (Mouza et al., 2014; Kabakci Yurdakul & Coklar, [2014)](#references). AIK is a key factor influencing the development of AIPACK in teachers (Celik, [2023)](#references). Through the AIPACK training model, the participants of the present study received an introduction to AIK through online videos, enabling them to gain knowledge on AI technologies and ethics dur- ing the initial AIK training phase. The present findings support the idea outlined by UNESCO (2024) that proficiency in one domain can translate into proficiency in another domain. In other words, the present findings indicate that teachers can leverage their AIK to more easily obtain AIPK, AICK, and AIPACK. Kim and Kwon ([2023)](#references) and Sun et al. (2022) have reported that inservice teachers often lack the AI knowledge required to use AI in support of their instruction.

The AIPACK model of the present study equipped the participants with essen- tial AI knowledge, thus improving their capacity to integrate AI into their teaching practice. No significant improvement in ethical awareness (a component of AIK) was noted in the participants. A possible explanation for this result is that the train- ing phase did not comprehensively address all aspects of AI ethics, such as fair- ness, transparency, accountability, and inclusiveness and lacked relevant case studies or regulations. Future research designs may involve group discussions on ethical issues, such as the fairness of using AI tools to automatically score student essays. The ISETs and PSETs did not significantly differ in their posttest AIK scores. This nonsignificant difference may be related to the fact that GAI is a novel technology and both groups had similar levels of prior knowledge on AIK prior to the training.

Second, the AIPK phase of the model provided the ISETs and PSETs with opportunities to construct knowledge about common AI-driven instructional tools, including AI learn- ing companions developed by Taiwan’s MOE; to strengthen their ability to integrate AI into their lesson plans and subject-specific materials; to use AI to automatically score or provide feedback on writing worksheets; and to use AI to obtain adaptive learning feed- back from students. These activities improved the ability of the participants to transfer their knowledge to future instructional contexts. All participants in this study exhibited improvements in AIPK. This may be because the AIPK phase covered essential pedagogi- cal concepts and offered opportunities for hands-on participation.

Third, in the AICK and AIPACK phases, the participants received instruction from three teachers who were modeling experts in Chinese, mathematics, and the natural sci- ence. In the AICK phase, the three expert teachers introduced AI-driven tools specific to their subject areas. In the AIPACK phase, in line with the principle of being a “modeler of practice,” the PSETs participants often emulated the instructional strategies and behav- iors of the experienced teachers they observed during training (Rozelle & Wilson, 2012). Numerous researchers have reported that effective modeling strategies in teacher educa- tion programs can facilitate the development of preservice teachers’ TPACK (Horzum, [2013;](#references) Wang et al., [2018)](#authors-and-affiliations). In the present study, the expert teachers demonstrated the AI competencies required for effective instruction in their fields and the effective selection of AI-driven tools for subject-specific instruction. Thus, such guidance and modeling can provide scaffolding that can effectively improve instructional competencies among teach- ers. The present findings indicate a significant improvement in AIPACK scores after train- ing, indicating that a well-designed training model can effectively improve the AI-related knowledge, AI-PK, AI-CK, and AI-PACK of elementary school teachers. The AIPACK model is effective because it requires all teachers in training to acquire knowledge on AI before they can acquire AIPK and AICK; thus, teachers from a non-STEM background can gain a conceptual foundation in AI before learning about the practical use of AI. There- fore, training programs for teachers should adopt the AIPACK model and also implement expert teacher modeling.

This study has several limitations. First, the sample size was small, and only two groups received the AIPACK training. Future studies should include more teachers to investi- gate the effectiveness of the AIPACK model and should provide more opportunities for teachers to practically apply their AIPACK in hands-on instruction. This would facilitate the development of appropriate curricula on AI competencies. In addition, the AIPACK model was implemented in an intensive summer program for inservice teachers who were not teaching at the time because students were on summer vacation. Moreover, because the preservice teachers were student teachers, they had limited opportunities to practically apply their AIPACK in instruction. Future studies should ensure that both inservice and preservice teachers have opportunities to implement AI-integrated subject-specific instruc- tion in authentic teaching contexts after receiving training. In addition, future studies should include teachers from different universities to elucidate differences in the influence of their AI competencies and knowledge on their willingness to adopt AI-integrated sub- ject-specific instruction in their courses. Another limitation of this study is the difference in delivery duration between the two participant groups. Because the ISETs hailed from different regions of Taiwan, they could only participate in an intensive PD course during summer or winter vacation, whereas the PSETs completed the course as part of their regu-

lar semester curriculum. This difference may have introduced confounding effects, such as variations in cognitive load, knowledge retention, and learning consolidation. Future research should standardize delivery schedules across groups or investigate the influence of different delivery durations on learning effectiveness. Furthermore, another limitation of this study is its sole use of quantitative data. Future research can further clarify the mechanism underlying the effectiveness of the AIPACK model by employing qualitative methods, such as interviews or participant observation, to determine the type of assistance they require to implement such instruction.

All participants in the present study majored in non-STEM subjects. Thus, they required instruction on fundamental AI concepts to help them design AI-integrated courses. The perspectives, attitudes, beliefs, and self-efficacy of teachers affect their knowledge, ability, behavior, and thinking and their way of interpreting the curricu- lum in their instructional practice. Therefore, research should be conducted to inves- tigate how the attitudes, beliefs, and competencies of teachers with respect to AI contribute to whether they use AI well if at all.
